work.title: The First Part of King Henry the Fourth
work.author: William Shakespeare

content.text: Enter a Carrier with a lantern in his hand.

lines.text: Heigh-ho! an it be not four by the day, I'll be hang'd. Charles' wain is over the new chimney, and yet our horse not pack'd.—What, ostler!
lines.plainText: Heighho an it be not four by the day I'll be hang'd Charles' wain is over the new chimney and yet our horse not pack'dWhat ostler

lines.text: [within.] Anon, anon.
lines.plainText: within Anon anon

lines.text: I prithee, Tom, beat Cut's saddle, put a few flocks in the point; poor jade is wrung in the withers out of all cess.
lines.plainText: I prithee Tom beat Cut's saddle put a few flocks in the point poor jade is wrung in the withers out of all cess

lines.text: Peas and beans are as dank here as a dog, and that is the next way to give poor jades the bots. This house is turned upside down since Robin ostler died.
lines.plainText: Peas and beans are as dank here as a dog and that is the next way to give poor jades the bots This house is turned upside down since Robin ostler died

lines.text: Poor fellow never joyed since the price of oats rose, it was the death of him.
lines.plainText: Poor fellow never joyed since the price of oats rose it was the death of him

lines.text: I think this be the most villainous house in all London road for fleas. I am stung like a tench.
lines.plainText: I think this be the most villainous house in all London road for fleas I am stung like a tench

lines.text: Like a tench! By the Mass, there is ne'er a king christen could be better bit than I have been since the first cock.
lines.plainText: Like a tench By the Mass there is ne'er a king christen could be better bit than I have been since the first cock

lines.text: Why, they will allow us ne'er a jordan, and then we leak in your chimney, and your chamber-lye breeds fleas like a loach.
lines.plainText: Why they will allow us ne'er a jordan and then we leak in your chimney and your chamberlye breeds fleas like a loach

lines.text: What, ostler! Come away and be hanged, come away.
lines.plainText: What ostler Come away and be hanged come away

lines.text: I have a gammon of bacon and two razes of ginger, to be delivered as far as Charing Cross.
lines.plainText: I have a gammon of bacon and two razes of ginger to be delivered as far as Charing Cross

lines.text: God's body! The turkeys in my pannier are quite starved.—What, ostler! A plague on thee! Hast thou never an eye in thy head? Canst not hear? An 'twere not as good deed as drink to break the pate on thee, I am a very villain. Come, and be hanged. Hast no faith in thee?
lines.plainText: God's body The turkeys in my pannier are quite starvedWhat ostler A plague on thee Hast thou never an eye in thy head Canst not hear An 'twere not as good deed as drink to break the pate on thee I am a very villain Come and be hanged Hast no faith in thee

lines.text: Good morrow, carriers. What's o'clock?
lines.plainText: Good morrow carriers What's o'clock

lines.text: I think it be two o'clock.
lines.plainText: I think it be two o'clock

lines.text: I prithee, lend me thy lantern, to see my gelding in the stable.
lines.plainText: I prithee lend me thy lantern to see my gelding in the stable

lines.text: Nay, by God, soft! I know a trick worth two of that, i'faith.
lines.plainText: Nay by God soft I know a trick worth two of that i'faith

lines.text: I pray thee, lend me thine.
lines.plainText: I pray thee lend me thine

lines.text: Ay, when? Canst tell? "Lend me thy lantern," quoth he! Marry, I'll see thee hanged first.
lines.plainText: Ay when Canst tell Lend me thy lantern quoth he Marry I'll see thee hanged first

lines.text: Sirrah carrier, what time do you mean to come to London?
lines.plainText: Sirrah carrier what time do you mean to come to London

lines.text: Time enough to go to bed with a candle, I warrant thee. Come, neighbour Mugs, we'll call up the gentlemen. They will along with company, for they have great charge.
lines.plainText: Time enough to go to bed with a candle I warrant thee Come neighbour Mugs we'll call up the gentlemen They will along with company for they have great charge

lines.text: What, ho! Chamberlain!
lines.plainText: What ho Chamberlain

lines.text: At hand, quoth pick-purse.
lines.plainText: At hand quoth pickpurse

lines.text: That's even as fair as "at hand, quoth the chamberlain," for thou variest no more from picking of purses than giving direction doth from labouring; thou layest the plot how.
lines.plainText: That's even as fair as at hand quoth the chamberlain for thou variest no more from picking of purses than giving direction doth from labouring thou layest the plot how

lines.text: Good morrow, Master Gadshill. It holds current that I told you yesternight: there's a franklin in the Wild of Kent hath brought three hundred marks with him in gold. I heard him tell it to one of his company last night at supper; a kind of auditor, one that hath abundance of charge too, God knows what. They are up already, and call for eggs and butter. They will away presently.
lines.plainText: Good morrow Master Gadshill It holds current that I told you yesternight there's a franklin in the Wild of Kent hath brought three hundred marks with him in gold I heard him tell it to one of his company last night at supper a kind of auditor one that hath abundance of charge too God knows what They are up already and call for eggs and butter They will away presently

lines.text: Sirrah, if they meet not with Saint Nicholas' clerks, I'll give thee this neck.
lines.plainText: Sirrah if they meet not with Saint Nicholas' clerks I'll give thee this neck

lines.text: No, I'll none of it. I pray thee, keep that for the hangman, for I know thou worshippest Saint Nicholas as truly as a man of falsehood may.
lines.plainText: No I'll none of it I pray thee keep that for the hangman for I know thou worshippest Saint Nicholas as truly as a man of falsehood may

lines.text: What talkest thou to me of the hangman? If I hang, I'll make a fat pair of gallows; for, if I hang, old Sir John hangs with me, and thou knowest he is no starveling. Tut, there are other Troyans that thou dream'st not of, the which for sport sake are content to do the profession some grace, that would, if matters should be looked into, for their own credit sake make all whole. I am joined with no foot-land-rakers, no long-staff sixpenny strikers, none of these mad mustachio purple-hued malt-worms, but with nobility and tranquillity, burgomasters and great oneyers, such as can hold in, such as will strike sooner than speak, and speak sooner than drink, and drink sooner than pray: and yet, zounds, I lie, for they pray continually to their saint the commonwealth, or rather not pray to her, but prey on her, for they ride up and down on her, and make her their boots.
lines.plainText: What talkest thou to me of the hangman If I hang I'll make a fat pair of gallows for if I hang old Sir John hangs with me and thou knowest he is no starveling Tut there are other Troyans that thou dream'st not of the which for sport sake are content to do the profession some grace that would if matters should be looked into for their own credit sake make all whole I am joined with no footlandrakers no longstaff sixpenny strikers none of these mad mustachio purplehued maltworms but with nobility and tranquillity burgomasters and great oneyers such as can hold in such as will strike sooner than speak and speak sooner than drink and drink sooner than pray and yet zounds I lie for they pray continually to their saint the commonwealth or rather not pray to her but prey on her for they ride up and down on her and make her their boots

lines.text: What, the commonwealth their boots? Will she hold out water in foul way?
lines.plainText: What the commonwealth their boots Will she hold out water in foul way

lines.text: She will, she will; justice hath liquored her. We steal as in a castle, cock-sure; we have the receipt of fern-seed, we walk invisible.
lines.plainText: She will she will justice hath liquored her We steal as in a castle cocksure we have the receipt of fernseed we walk invisible

lines.text: Nay, by my faith, I think you are more beholding to the night than to fern-seed for your walking invisible.
lines.plainText: Nay by my faith I think you are more beholding to the night than to fernseed for your walking invisible

lines.text: Give me thy hand. Thou shalt have a share in our purchase, as I am a true man.
lines.plainText: Give me thy hand Thou shalt have a share in our purchase as I am a true man

lines.text: Nay, rather let me have it, as you are a false thief.
lines.plainText: Nay rather let me have it as you are a false thief

lines.text: Go to; homo is a common name to all men. Bid the ostler bring my gelding out of the stable. Farewell, you muddy knave.
lines.plainText: Go to homo is a common name to all men Bid the ostler bring my gelding out of the stable Farewell you muddy knave
